1149.title: The science of men
1149.hook: scholars wrote lives of the narrators, to test each one
1149.howItsDone: Hadith scholars consult biographical dictionaries of narrators, the books of rijal, to check each name in a chain for honesty, memory and whom they met, a field called al-jarh wa al-ta'dil.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mutawatir, a report carried by so many chains that it gives certainty.

A story is told about the hadith scholar Ali ibn al-Madini. Someone asked him about a narrator, and the narrator was his own father. He hesitated, and said: ask someone else. They pressed him. And he answered, as the story goes: this is the religion. My father is weak. Whatever the details, the story shows what a whole field of study asked of people: a son choosing accuracy over family pride. Behind that answer stood a library of judgments about people. Today, the science of men.
screen: `ASKED ABOUT HIS OWN FATHER.` → `THIS IS THE RELIGION.` → `A LIBRARY ABOUT PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Rijal means men, and in hadith study it names the narrators themselves, the people in the chains. Despite the word, the books include women who narrated too. Why it began: in the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the early scholar Ibn Sirin is quoted saying, in effect, people didn't use to ask about chains. Then came the time of turmoil, and they said: name your men for us. And again: this knowledge is religion, so look at whom you take your religion from. What the books record: entry after entry, narrator by narrator. Where he lived. Whom he heard from, and who heard from him. Whether he traveled. Was he truthful? Was his memory precise, or did it slip, or fade late in life? Did he write his reports down, and keep the pages safe? The field has a blunt name: al-jarh wa al-ta'dil, wounding and vouching. Each narrator could be wounded by a scholar's criticism, or vouched for. Then a hard question, faced openly. Isn't talking about a man's flaws a kind of backbiting? Imam Muslim answers in that same introduction: exposing a narrator's weakness, to protect what's said in the Prophet's name, isn't forbidden backbiting. It's a duty. Out of this came books of narrators that students of hadith still open. When a scholar grades a report, this is the shelf behind the grade.
screen: `RIJAL: THE PEOPLE IN THE CHAINS.` · `NAME YOUR MEN FOR US.` · `WOUNDING AND VOUCHING.` · `NOT BACKBITING, A DUTY.`

segments.voice: Pick one voice you trust for information, a news outlet, a teacher, a channel, a friend who always knows things, and quietly ask the rijal questions: where do they get what they tell me, have they been wrong and said so, do details drift, do they have a reason to shade the story? You're not putting them on trial, only writing a short entry in your own book of narrators. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in judging.
Rijal. Literally men: the narrators in the chains, and the science of studying who each one was and whether he can be trusted. Today's word.
Your line: who was he? Behind every grade, a shelf of lives. Same time tomorrow.

1150.title: The traveling scholars
1150.hook: scholars journeyed far to hear one hadith from its source
1150.howItsDone: Students of hadith and Islamic learning have long traveled to study with teachers in person, a practice called the rihla, and some still travel to receive a chain of transmission directly from a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rijal, the science of men: who each narrator was, and whether he could be trusted.

One line in Sahih al-Bukhari, almost tucked away in a chapter heading. Jabir ibn Abdullah, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ, traveled a month's distance to Abdullah ibn Unays, for a single hadith. Not for trade. Not for war. One report. Fuller tellings of the story, outside Bukhari, add the details: Jabir buys a camel, saddles up, and rides to hear the report himself rather than take it secondhand. Today, the traveling scholars.
screen: `A MONTH'S DISTANCE.` → `FOR A SINGLE HADITH.` → `NOT SECONDHAND.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, in the Book of Knowledge, the chapter on going out in search of knowledge names Jabir's journey, and the report placed beneath it is about a prophet. Moses went looking for a man with knowledge he didn't have. The Qur'an gives his resolve, in Pickthall's words: "I will not give up until I reach the point where the two rivers meet, though I march on for ages." A companion and a prophet in one chapter: travel for learning sits in old company. Why not take it secondhand? Because every link in the chain is a place for something to slip, as the scholars knew. Hear it from the person who heard it, and the chain gets shorter and the path clearer. Scholars of hadith prized a shorter chain, and some traveled for that alone. The journey became a tradition of its own. Students moved between cities to sit with the teachers there, to compare what they'd heard, to check a report against another chain. It even has a name, rihla, and the scholar al-Khatib al-Baghdadi wrote a book gathering these journeys in search of hadith. What did they carry home? Not souvenirs. Notebooks. And the habit behind them is spelled out in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: whoever travels a road seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a road to paradise. By that hadith, the road to learning is itself counted.
screen: `A COMPANION, AND A PROPHET.` · `WHY NOT SECONDHAND?` · `RIHLA: THE JOURNEY FOR HADITH.` · `A ROAD MADE EASY.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've only ever taken secondhand, a question about your faith, your family's history, your work, and ask who holds it firsthand: a teacher, an elder, a grandparent, a scholar at the mosque or the library across town. Picture the journey, even if it's twenty minutes on a bus or a phone call across an ocean, and the one question you'd bring. If you pray, you can ask for an easy road.
The traveling scholars. Companions and students who rode far to hear a report from its source, so the chain would be shorter and surer. Today's word.
Your line: a journey for one report. Shorter chains, surer words. Tomorrow: exposing the fabrications.

1151.title: Exposing the fabrications
1151.hook: fabricated reports spread, and scholars worked hard to expose them
1151.howItsDone: Hadith scholars identify fabricated reports by examining chains, narrators, dates and texts, and compiled books of forgeries; Muslim teachers today often caution against sharing sayings attributed to the Prophet without a source and a grade.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the traveling scholars, who rode far to hear a report from its source.

A man stands in a gathering and says he heard a certain shaykh, in a certain city. He names the shaykh, the street, the season. Very convincing. A scholar in the room asks one quiet question: in what year did you hear him? The man answers. And the scholar says: that shaykh had already died by then. The report collapses. Scenes like this are told about the hadith scholars, and the early scholar Sufyan al-Thawri is reported to have put it simply: when the narrators used lies, we used history against them. Today, exposing the fabrications.
screen: `A CONVINCING STORY.` → `IN WHAT YEAR?` → `HISTORY AGAINST LIES.`

segments.voice: First, the warning. Three days ago we met the report carried by so many chains: whoever lies about the Prophet ﷺ on purpose, let him take his seat in the Fire. The introduction to Sahih Muslim has a quieter one, aimed not at the forger but at the forwarder: it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears. So the duty runs two ways. Don't invent, and don't simply repeat. Why people forged: the scholars were frank about it. Some wanted to win an argument between factions. Some were storytellers after a bigger crowd. Some wanted favor from a ruler. And some, as the scholars tell it, meant well. They report a man who admitted inventing reports about the reward for reciting each surah of the Qur'an, because he thought people were drifting from it. Good intentions didn't save the report. A lie about the Prophet stayed a lie. How they caught them: every tool from this block came out. The chain: did these people meet? The narrators: who was he, and how was his memory? The dates: was the shaykh even alive? The text: does it promise a mountain for a pebble, or clash with the Qur'an? And they wrote it down. Scholars compiled whole books of fabricated reports, such as Ibn al-Jawzi's collection of forgeries, so a false saying could be named and recognized, not quietly forgotten and later revived. A forged hadith in a book of forgeries is a lie with a warning label tied around its neck.
screen: `DON'T INVENT. DON'T JUST REPEAT.` · `WHY PEOPLE FORGED.` · `HOW THEY CAUGHT THEM.` · `A BOOK OF FORGERIES.`

segments.voice: Recall the last message that began with something like "the Prophet said", "scientists say" or "a famous person once said". Run it through the scholars' tools: who sent it and where did they get it, is there a source, does it promise too much, does a date not fit? If you can't answer, you have your answer: not yet.
Exposing the fabrications. The scholars' work of catching forged reports, by chain, by narrator, by date and by text, and naming them in books so they couldn't hide. Today's word.
Your line: they checked. Good intentions never saved a forged report. See you next time.

1152.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
1152.hook: a book that opens with intention, built from reports al-Bukhari judged sound
1152.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims study Sahih al-Bukhari with teachers, cite its hadith by number, and in some communities gather to read it aloud from beginning to end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: exposing the fabrications, and how scholars caught forged reports by chain, narrator, date and text.

Actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. You traced those words through their chain a week ago. Now look at where they sit. Open Sahih al-Bukhari to its first page, and that's where it begins: a report from Umar ibn al-Khattab that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said those words. Before a single ruling about prayer, or fasting, or buying and selling, the reader meets a quiet question. Why are you here, opening this book? All that checking had to end up somewhere. One of the places it ended up is today's word. Sahih al-Bukhari.
screen: `ACTIONS ARE JUDGED BY INTENTIONS.` → `THE FIRST PAGE.` → `WHERE ALL THE CHECKING LED.`

segments.voice: You met al-Bukhari's journey long ago. Today, his book. Sahih means sound, healthy, whole: the top of the scale. Al-Bukhari is the man, Muhammad ibn Isma'il, called after Bukhara, the city he came from. People often just call his book the Sahih, the sound one. The sifting: tradition says al-Bukhari heard a vast number of reports on his travels and kept only a small share, the ones whose chains passed his test, each narrator trustworthy and careful, each known to have heard from the person before him. Tradition also says that before writing each hadith into the book, he washed and prayed. Whether every detail of that story is exact or not, it shows what the book meant to the people who told it. The headings: al-Bukhari set the reports under chapter titles he wrote himself, and those titles are often small arguments. A heading states a point, and the hadith beneath it back the point up. Scholars have a saying that al-Bukhari's understanding is in his headings. So the book isn't only a store of reports. It's also one careful reader's reading of them. The place it holds: in Sunni scholarship, this book holds a special trust, and with tomorrow's book it makes up the pair called the two Sahihs. Some communities gather to read it aloud, cover to cover, and celebrate when they finish. Shia Muslims have their own collections and their own science of grading, which this path reaches in a few days. And remember where it starts. Before the rulings, the question of intention.
screen: `SAHIH: SOUND, HEALTHY, WHOLE.` · `A SMALL SHARE, CAREFULLY KEPT.` · `HIS UNDERSTANDING IS IN HIS HEADINGS.` · `READ ALOUD, COVER TO COVER.`

Find the one place where the second half would help most, keep quiet, and hold that place in mind.

Your line: the sound collection. Something good, or nothing at all. Rest well.

1153.title: Sahih Muslim
1153.hook: Muslim's Sahih, known for its careful arrangement
1153.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims study Sahih Muslim alongside Sahih al-Bukhari, and teachers often use its gathered chains to show students how one hadith came down in several wordings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sahih al-Bukhari, the sound collection, which opens with a hadith on intentions.

A desk, a lamp, and a stack of notes. One saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has reached you along several chains of narrators, each wording it a little differently. One adds a detail. One gives the whole scene; another, only the saying. So where do they go in your book? Scattered, a piece here and a piece there, wherever each fits a topic? Or all together, side by side, so a reader can see every version and spot exactly where they differ? One scholar chose the second way, and it's what his book is known for. Today, Sahih Muslim.
screen: `ONE SAYING, SEVERAL CHAINS.` → `SCATTER THEM, OR GATHER THEM?` → `SAHIH MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, from the city of Nishapur. Muslim here is his name, not only his faith. Tradition says he studied with al-Bukhari and held him in deep respect. Two students of one science, two books with the same name, sahih, sound. Together they're called the two Sahihs. Second, the arrangement. Al-Bukhari sometimes divided a hadith across his book, a piece under each heading where it proved a point. Muslim, for the most part, kept a hadith in one place and laid its chains and wordings next to each other. For a student, that's a gift: you can watch one saying travel down several roads and see the exact place where a word changes. Third, the doorway. Before the hadith begin, Muslim wrote an introduction. In it he explains why he takes reports only from people known to be reliable, and he warns against passing things on carelessly. He records a saying of the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak: the chain of narrators is part of the religion, and without it, anyone could say whatever they liked. Everything from last week, in one line. Fourth, one hadith from inside. In Muslim's book, the Prophet says that Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but looks at your hearts and your deeds. Hearts and deeds, together. Scholars have weighed the two Sahihs against each other, and not all of them came down on the same side. This path takes them as a pair.
screen: `MUSLIM IBN AL-HAJJAJ, OF NISHAPUR.` · `EVERY CHAIN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE CHAIN IS PART OF THE RELIGION.` · `HEARTS AND DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Let today's hadith land: Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds. Recall the last time you sized someone up by how they looked, the clothes, the face, the car, then turn it around: what did you spend on your appearance this week, and what on your heart? No verdict, just look, the way you'd look at a receipt; if you pray, you can carry this hadith into your next prayer.
Sahih Muslim. The second of the two Sahihs, where each hadith's chains and wordings are gathered in one place, side by side. Today's word.
Your line: the second sahih. What Allah looks at: hearts and deeds, not faces. Back tomorrow.

1154.title: The four Sunan
1154.hook: Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah complete the six books
1154.howItsDone: Students of hadith learn the six books by name, and when a hadith is cited from one of the Sunan, a careful teacher checks its grade as well as its source.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sahih Muslim, where each hadith's chains sit side by side, and the two Sahihs as a pair.

Smiling in your brother's face is charity. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that, in a report from a book we haven't opened yet: the collection of al-Tirmidhi. The two Sahihs aren't the whole shelf. Beside them stand four more books, and together the six make up a set known as the six books: al-Bukhari, Muslim, and four collections with a plainer name. Today, the four Sunan.
screen: `A SMILE IS CHARITY.` → `ANOTHER BOOK.` → `FOUR MORE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Sunan is the plural of sunnah: ways, practices. These books are laid out like a handbook of daily life. Purity, prayer, charity, fasting, trade, marriage, food. Want to know what the Prophet did about something practical? Open a Sunan to that chapter and start reading. Second, the names. Four compilers, each known by a short name: Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah. Say them like a roll call. Each book has its own habits. Al-Tirmidhi we met a week ago, stepping out after a report to give his verdict on it. He often also names which scholars acted on it. Third, the honest part. Sunan doesn't mean sahih. These books hold reports graded sound, reports graded good, and some graded weak, and the compilers often say so themselves. That's why this path spent days on grading before it reached the books. A hadith's book tells you where it's kept. Its grade tells you how firm it is. You want both. Fourth, the set. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, plus these four, are called the six books, al-kutub al-sitta. Scholars didn't all agree on who belongs in the sixth seat; some placed Malik's Muwatta there instead of Ibn Majah, and tomorrow we meet Malik himself. Next time you see a hadith cited with a book name and a number, you may recognize the name.

segments.voice: Count the six on your fingers, one name for each breath: on one hand, al-Bukhari and Muslim, the two Sahihs; on the other, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. 1155.title: Malik and Ahmad
1155.hook: the Muwatta of Malik and the Musnad of Ahmad, early and vast
1155.tomorrow: The four books of the Shia
1155.howItsDone: Followers of the Maliki school study the Muwatta closely, and scholars across schools use Ahmad's Musnad as a large reference archive of reports arranged by Companion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four Sunan, which with the two Sahihs make up the six books.

Medina. A teacher sits in the city where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lived and was buried, with students gathered around him and a book he has written. Tradition says he kept working on it, revising and trimming, for a long time before he was satisfied. He called it al-Muwatta: the trodden path, the way made smooth by the people who walked it before. His name was Malik ibn Anas. Today, two collections that stand beside the six books and are counted among the early ones. Malik and Ahmad.
screen: `A TEACHER IN MEDINA.` → `THE TRODDEN PATH.` → `BESIDE THE SIX BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the Muwatta. It's arranged by topics of law, like the Sunan, but it holds more than the Prophet's words. Next to them, Malik records what Companions did, what the people of Medina practiced, and his own judgment on the question. For Malik, the way the city of the Prophet actually lived was itself a kind of witness. One short report from it is easy to carry: the Prophet said that he was sent to perfect good character. Second, a line of teachers. Tradition says al-Shafi'i studied the Muwatta with Malik, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal later studied with al-Shafi'i. Founders of schools of law, each one sitting in front of the one before. Third, the Musnad. Ahmad's book is vast, and built a completely different way. Musnad means supported, propped up by a chain. Instead of chapters on prayer or trade, it's arranged by Companion: all the reports that came through one Companion, then all through the next. Want what Abu Bakr narrated? It's together. Want everything about prayer? You'll have to hunt through the whole book. Ahmad wasn't building a handbook. He was building an archive. Fourth, the people behind the books. Tradition remembers both men holding firm when rulers of their day pressed them to say or do what they believed was wrong, and both paid for it. A collection is never only paper. It's a life spent listening, and sometimes a life spent refusing.
screen: `THE MUWATTA: HADITH AND MEDINA'S PRACTICE.` · `MALIK, AL-SHAFI'I, AHMAD.` · `THE MUSNAD: ARRANGED BY COMPANION.` · `A LIFE SPENT LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Say the Muwatta's line slowly, in three pieces: sent, to perfect, good character. Notice what it doesn't say: not sent to win arguments, not sent to be admired. All the care of these weeks, the biographies, the journeys, the fakes exposed, was for lines like this one, so bring to mind one moment this week when your own character slipped, and one when it held, and look at both without a verdict.
Malik and Ahmad. The Muwatta, the trodden path of Medina, and the Musnad, the reports arranged by the Companion who told them. Today's word.
Your line: early collections. Two more shelves that stand beside the six books. That's the week.
